---
title: "Intertemporal Equilibrium with Production and Endogenous Interest Rates"
---

## The $3\times2$ Model

In structural equilibrium models, money is usually treated as an ad valorem claim, and the interest rate is usually treated as an ad valorem claim rate [@liwu2019e, chapter 7]. This example considers a finite-horizon intertemporal equilibrium with production and endogenous interest rates. There are three types of dated commodities---product, labor, and money---and two types of economic agents---firm and consumer.

Assume the following:

1. The economy operates for $n_p\geq3$ periods, indexed by $1,\ldots,n_p$. Production takes place in periods $i=1,\ldots,n_p-1$. Production in period $i$ produces product $i+1$, which is available in period $i+1$. Accordingly, the dated products are product $2,\ldots,n_p$, while the dated labor and money commodities are labor $1,\ldots,n_p-1$ and money $1,\ldots,n_p-1$. There is no product 1 commodity in the model; the first product generated by production is product 2. Thus, there are $3(n_p-1)$ dated commodities. There is one firm activity in each of the first $n_p-1$ periods and one consumer. Product 2 is the numeraire.
2. In production period $i$, the firm uses labor $l_i$ to produce product $i+1$ according to

$$
y_i=\alpha_i l_i,
\qquad
\alpha_i>0
$$

Let $y_i$ also denote the firm's activity level, measured by output. Thus, producing $y_i$ units of product $i+1$ requires $y_i/\alpha_i$ units of labor $i$. Before production, the firm presells product $i+1$ and uses money $i$ to purchase labor $i$.

3. The consumer has the intertemporal Cobb--Douglas utility function

$$
u=\prod_{i=1}^{n_p-1}c_{i+1}^{\beta_i}
$$

where $c_{i+1}$ denotes consumption of product $i+1$, produced in period $i$. The expenditure shares are strictly decreasing over production periods,

$$
\beta_1>\beta_2>\cdots>\beta_{n_p-1}>0,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n_p-1}\beta_i=1
$$

The consumer is endowed with $\omega_i>0$ units of labor $i$, $i=1,\ldots,n_p-1$. The decreasing-share assumption will ensure strictly positive equilibrium interest rates in all nonterminal production periods.
4. The consumer is endowed with one unit of money in each production period $i=1,\ldots,n_p-1$. Let $p_{m_i}$ denote the price of money $i$. We restrict attention to equilibria with strictly positive nonterminal interest rates,

$$
r_i>0,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
$$

while the terminal condition is

$$
r_{n_p-1}=+\infty
$$

For the terminal production period, define the finite interest-inclusive product price

$$
\tilde p_{n_p}
:=
\lim_{r_{n_p-1}\rightarrow+\infty}
(1+r_{n_p-1})p_{n_p}
$$

This variable allows the terminal demands to be written directly without introducing an infinite interest rate into the equilibrium system.

For the four-period case, $n_p=4$, there are three production periods. Let

$$
\mathbf p
=
\left(
1,p_3,p_4,
p_{l_1},p_{l_2},p_{l_3},
p_{m_1},p_{m_2},p_{m_3}
\right)^\top
$$

let $\mathbf y=(y_1,y_2,y_3)^\top$ denote firm activity levels, and let $w$ denote consumer income. The consumer's income is the value of the labor and money endowments,

$$
w
=
\sum_{i=1}^3p_{l_i}\omega_i
+
\sum_{i=1}^3p_{m_i}
$$

With rows representing product 2--4, labor 1--3, and money 1--3, and columns representing the three firms and the consumer, respectively, the demand matrix is

$$
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,\mathbf y,w,r_1,r_2,\tilde p_4)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0&0&0&\dfrac{\beta_1w}{1+r_1}\\[6pt]
0&0&0&\dfrac{\beta_2w}{(1+r_2)p_3}\\[6pt]
0&0&0&\dfrac{\beta_3w}{\tilde p_4}\\[6pt]
\dfrac{y_1}{\alpha_1}&0&0&0\\[6pt]
0&\dfrac{y_2}{\alpha_2}&0&0\\[6pt]
0&0&\dfrac{y_3}{\alpha_3}&0\\[6pt]
\dfrac{r_1p_{l_1}y_1}{\alpha_1p_{m_1}}&0&0&
\dfrac{\beta_1wr_1}{(1+r_1)p_{m_1}}\\[8pt]
0&\dfrac{r_2p_{l_2}y_2}{\alpha_2p_{m_2}}&0&
\dfrac{\beta_2wr_2}{(1+r_2)p_{m_2}}\\[8pt]
0&0&0&\dfrac{\beta_3w}{p_{m_3}}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

and the supply matrix is

$$
\mathbf S(\mathbf y)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
y_1&0&0&0\\
0&y_2&0&0\\
0&0&y_3&0\\
0&0&0&\omega_1\\
0&0&0&\omega_2\\
0&0&0&\omega_3\\
0&0&0&1\\
0&0&0&1\\
0&0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

The third firm's zero money demand is a terminal-limit result rather than an additional assumption. As the terminal interest rate tends to infinity, the terminal product price and the third-period labor price both tend to zero in a way that makes the firm's money demand vanish. Under the same terminal-limit treatment, the consumer's terminal-period product and money demands are written directly in terms of $\tilde p_4$ and $p_{m_3}$.

For each nonterminal production period, labor- and product-market clearing, together with the firm's revenue-expenditure balance condition, determine the firm's equilibrium money demand. Combining the firm's and consumer's money demands with money-market clearing gives

$$
p_{m_i}^*
=
\beta_iw^*
\frac{
r_i^*(r_i^*+2)
}{
(1+r_i^*)^2
},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
$$

Under the terminal condition, the terminal firm's money demand vanishes, while the consumer holds the entire unit of terminal money. Hence,

$$
p_{m_{n_p-1}}^*
=
\beta_{n_p-1}w^*
$$

These money-price relations provide the basis for deriving the backward recursion for the endogenous equilibrium interest rates.


## Analytical Solution for the Endogenous Interest Rates

The endogenous interest rates are determined by the equilibrium values of dated money. Define the tail value of money prices by

$$
v_i
:=
\sum_{j=i}^{n_p-1}p_{m_j}^*
$$

For each nonterminal period, the ad valorem claim-rate relation is

$$
r_i^*
=
\frac{p_{m_i}^*}{v_{i+1}},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
$$

Since

$$
v_i=p_{m_i}^*+v_{i+1}
$$

we have

$$
1+r_i^*
=
\frac{v_i}{v_{i+1}}
$$

Normalize the tail value by consumer income:

$$
g_i
:=
\frac{v_i}{w^*}
$$

The terminal value is

$$
g_{n_p-1}=\beta_{n_p-1}
$$

and

$$
1+r_i^*
=
\frac{g_i}{g_{i+1}}
$$

Using

$$
\frac{p_{m_i}^*}{w^*}
=
r_i^*g_{i+1}
$$

together with the money-market expression gives

$$
g_i^2-\beta_i g_i-\beta_i g_{i+1}=0
$$

Thus, the positive root yields the backward recursion

$$
g_i
=
\frac{
\beta_i+
\sqrt{
\beta_i^2+4\beta_i g_{i+1}
}
}{2},
\qquad
i=n_p-2,\ldots,1
$$

with

$$
g_{n_p-1}=\beta_{n_p-1}
$$

Once the sequence $g_i$ is obtained, the nonterminal equilibrium interest rates follow from

$$
r_i^*
=
\frac{g_i}{g_{i+1}}-1,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
$$

The decreasing-share assumption guarantees that these interest rates are strictly positive. To see this, note first that

$$
g_{n_p-1}=\beta_{n_p-1}<2\beta_{n_p-1}
$$

Suppose $g_{i+1}<2\beta_{i+1}$. Since $\beta_i>\beta_{i+1}$,

$$
g_{i+1}<2\beta_i
$$

Using

$$
g_i^2-\beta_i g_i-\beta_i g_{i+1}=0
$$

and evaluating the left-hand side at $g_{i+1}$ and $2\beta_i$ shows that the positive root satisfies

$$
g_{i+1}<g_i<2\beta_i
$$

This establishes the induction step. Proceeding backward therefore gives

$$
g_1>g_2>\cdots>g_{n_p-1}>0
$$

and hence

$$
r_i^*>0,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
$$

Thus, for any finite $n_p$, the backward recursion directly determines the strictly positive nonterminal equilibrium interest rates under the maintained assumption $\beta_1>\beta_2>\cdots>\beta_{n_p-1}>0$. The productivity parameters $\alpha_i$ and labor endowments $\omega_i$ affect equilibrium quantities and prices but do not enter the interest-rate recursion.

### Common Nonterminal Interest Rate

A useful special case imposes a common nonterminal equilibrium interest rate,

$$
r_i^*=r>0,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
$$

Then

$$
g_i=(1+r)g_{i+1}
$$

and the share parameters satisfy

$$
\beta_i
=
\beta_{n_p-1}
\frac{
(1+r)^{n_p-i}
}{
r+2
},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
$$

Together with $\sum_{i=1}^{n_p-1}\beta_i=1$, this determines the complete sequence of shares. Under the maintained decreasing-share assumption, the common-rate specification must also satisfy

$$
\beta_{n_p-2}>\beta_{n_p-1}
$$

which, using the expression above, is equivalent to

$$
\frac{(1+r)^2}{r+2}>1
$$

or

$$
r>\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}
$$

For earlier periods, $\beta_i/\beta_{i+1}=1+r>1$, so this terminal-adjacent condition is sufficient for the entire sequence to be strictly decreasing. In particular, when $r=1$,

$$
\beta_i
=
\frac{
2^{n_p-i}
}{
2^{n_p}-1
},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
$$

and

$$
\beta_{n_p-1}
=
\frac{3}{2^{n_p}-1}
$$

which gives

$$
r_1^*=\cdots=r_{n_p-2}^*=1
$$

## Numerical Example

Consider the four-period case, $n_p=4$, with three production periods and

$$
\beta_1=\frac8{15},
\qquad
\beta_2=\frac4{15},
\qquad
\beta_3=\frac15
$$

and

$$
\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha_3=1,
\qquad
\omega_1=\omega_2=\omega_3=100
$$

The recursive solution gives

$$
r_1^*=r_2^*=1,
\qquad
r_3=+\infty
$$

Consumer income is

$$
w^*=375
$$

The terminal interest-inclusive product price is

$$
\tilde p_4^*
=
\frac{\beta_3w^*}{\alpha_3\omega_3}
=
\frac34
$$

and the equilibrium commodity price vector, interpreted in the limiting sense for the terminal product and labor prices, is

$$
\mathbf p^*
=
\left(
1,\frac12,0,
\frac12,\frac14,0,
150,75,75
\right)^\top
$$

Indeed,

$$
w^*
=
\frac12(100)
+
\frac14(100)
+
150+75+75
=
375
$$

The equilibrium output and consumption quantities are

$$
y_i^*=c_{i+1}^*=100,
\qquad
i=1,2,3
$$

The firms' money holdings are

$$
(h_1^{f*},h_2^{f*},h_3^{f*})
=
\left(
\frac13,\frac13,0
\right)
$$

and the consumer's money holdings are

$$
(h_1^{c*},h_2^{c*},h_3^{c*})
=
\left(
\frac23,\frac23,1
\right)
$$

Hence, every dated money market clears.

The equilibrium demand and supply matrices are

$$
\mathbf D^*
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0&0&0&100\\
0&0&0&100\\
0&0&0&100\\
100&0&0&0\\
0&100&0&0\\
0&0&100&0\\
\frac13&0&0&\frac23\\
0&\frac13&0&\frac23\\
0&0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

and

$$
\mathbf S^*
=
\begin{bmatrix}
100&0&0&0\\
0&100&0&0\\
0&0&100&0\\
0&0&0&100\\
0&0&0&100\\
0&0&0&100\\
0&0&0&1\\
0&0&0&1\\
0&0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

## Numerical Solution

The model can be solved using the GEMB framework for an arbitrary total number of periods $n_p$. The variables $r_1,\ldots,r_{n_p-2}$ are determined jointly with commodity prices and agent activity levels. The terminal infinite interest rate is not introduced directly. Instead, the program uses the finite terminal interest-inclusive product price

$$
\tilde p_{n_p}
=
\lim_{r_{n_p-1}\rightarrow+\infty}
(1+r_{n_p-1})p_{n_p}
$$

A `ConditionAgentSpec` introduces $r_1,\ldots,r_{n_p-2}$ and $\tilde p_{n_p}$ as endogenous variables. The interest-rate relation is

$$
r_i
=
\frac{
p_{m_i}
}{
\displaystyle\sum_{j=i+1}^{n_p-1}p_{m_j}
},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
$$

For numerical implementation, it can equivalently be written without division as

$$
r_i
\sum_{j=i+1}^{n_p-1}p_{m_j}
-p_{m_i}
=0,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
$$

For a nonterminal firm, an activity level $y_i$ implies labor demand $y_i/\alpha_i$ and money holdings

$$
h_i^f
=
\frac{
r_i p_{l_i}y_i
}{
\alpha_i p_{m_i}
},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
$$

The terminal firm is represented by the limiting form associated with $r_{n_p-1}\rightarrow+\infty$, so its money holdings approach zero.

Given income $w$, the consumer's nonterminal product demand and money holdings are

$$
c_{i+1}
=
\frac{
\beta_iw
}{
(1+r_i)p_{i+1}
}
$$

and

$$
h_i^c
=
\frac{
r_i\beta_iw
}{
(1+r_i)p_{m_i}
},
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n_p-2
$$

The terminal demands are represented by the finite limiting expressions

$$
c_{n_p}
=
\frac{
\beta_{n_p-1}w
}{
\tilde p_{n_p}
}
$$

and

$$
h_{n_p-1}^c
=
\frac{
\beta_{n_p-1}w
}{
p_{m_{n_p-1}}
}
$$

The program can generate the common-rate share parameterization above for arbitrary total period count $n_p$ and solve the resulting equilibrium system numerically. Under the maintained decreasing-share assumption, a common rate should satisfy $r>(\sqrt5-1)/2$; the numerical example uses $r=1$.

## Infinite-Horizon Equilibrium

Consider an infinite-horizon version of the model, with production periods indexed by $i=1,2,\ldots$. Production in period $i$ uses labor $i$ to produce product $i+1$. There is no terminal production period and hence no terminal infinite-interest-rate condition.

Assume the following:

1. The consumer has geometric expenditure shares

$$
\beta_i=(1-\rho)\rho^{i-1},
\qquad
0<\rho<1,
\qquad
i=1,2,\ldots
$$

so that

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\beta_i=1
$$

2. Productivity and labor endowment are constant over time:

$$
\alpha_i=\alpha>0,
\qquad
\omega_i=\omega>0
$$

3. The consumer is endowed with one unit of money in each production period. Product 2 is the numeraire.

We seek an equilibrium with finite consumer income $w^*>0$ and summable dated-money prices. Define

$$
v_i=\sum_{j=i}^{\infty}p_{m_j}^*,
\qquad
g_i=\frac{v_i}{w^*}
$$

The ad valorem claim-rate relation implies

$$
r_i^*=\frac{p_{m_i}^*}{v_{i+1}},
\qquad
1+r_i^*=\frac{g_i}{g_{i+1}}
$$

As in the finite-horizon model, money-market clearing gives

$$
\frac{p_{m_i}^*}{w^*}
=
\beta_i
\frac{r_i^*(r_i^*+2)}{(1+r_i^*)^2}
$$

For strictly positive interest rates, these relations yield

$$
g_i^2-\beta_i g_i-\beta_i g_{i+1}=0
$$

Since $\beta_{i+1}=\rho\beta_i$, a proportional solution $g_i=C\beta_i$ satisfies

$$
C=1+\rho
$$

Thus,

$$
g_i=(1+\rho)\beta_i
$$

and the equilibrium interest rate is constant:

$$
r_i^*=\frac1\rho-1>0,
\qquad
i=1,2,\ldots
$$

Equivalently, writing $r=1/\rho-1$, the expenditure shares are

$$
\beta_i=\frac{r}{(1+r)^i}
$$

The corresponding dated-money prices satisfy

$$
p_{m_i}^*
=
w^*(g_i-g_{i+1})
=
w^*(1-\rho^2)\beta_i
$$

These prices are positive and summable. Moreover,

$$
\sum_{j=i}^{\infty}p_{m_j}^*
=
w^*(1+\rho)\beta_i
=
w^*g_i
$$

so the proposed sequence is consistent with the definition of the tail value, and $v_i\rightarrow0$ as $i\rightarrow\infty$.

Labor- and product-market clearing give constant equilibrium output and consumption:

$$
y_i^*=c_{i+1}^*=\alpha\omega
$$

Taking product 2 as the numeraire yields

$$
w^*=\frac{\alpha\omega}{\rho(1-\rho)}
$$

The equilibrium commodity prices are

$$
p_{i+1}^*=\rho^{i-1},
\qquad
p_{l_i}^*=\alpha\rho^i,
\qquad
p_{m_i}^*
=
\frac{1-\rho^2}{\rho}\alpha\omega\rho^{i-1}
$$

They satisfy the consumer-income identity

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_{l_i}^*\omega
+
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_{m_i}^*
=
\frac{\alpha\omega}{\rho(1-\rho)}
=
w^*
$$

The equilibrium money holdings are also constant over time:

$$
h_i^{f*}=\frac{\rho}{1+\rho},
\qquad
h_i^{c*}=\frac1{1+\rho}
$$

Thus, every dated money market clears. The infinite-horizon equilibrium has constant output, consumption, and money holdings, a constant interest rate determined by $\rho$, and geometrically declining dated-commodity prices.

## Steady State: A $3\times2$ Equality-Form Wide-Sense Structural Equilibrium Model

The infinite-horizon steady state can be represented by a finite-dimensional equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model.

Assume the following:

1. There are three commodity types: product, labor, and money; and two economic-agent types: firm and consumer. Product is the numeraire.
2. The consumer supplies $\omega>0$ units of labor and one unit of money, and consumes only product.
3. The firm uses labor to produce product according to

$$
y=\alpha l,
\qquad
\alpha>0
$$

4. Let $\rho\in(0,1)$ denote the intertemporal discount factor. The steady-state interest rate is

$$
r=\frac1{\rho}-1
$$

Let

$$
\mathbf p=(1,p_l,p_m)^\top
$$

where $p_l$ and $p_m$ are the prices of labor and money, respectively. The prices of money represent the interest on a unit of money.
For a given output level $y$, labor demand is

$$
l=\frac{y}{\alpha}
$$

Money is required for labor purchases by the firm and product purchases by the consumer. Accordingly, the demand and supply matrices are

$$
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,y,c)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0
&
c
\\[6pt]
\displaystyle\frac{y}{\alpha}
&
0
\\[10pt]
\displaystyle\frac{rp_l}{p_m}\frac{y}{\alpha}
&
\displaystyle\frac{rc}{p_m}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

and

$$
\mathbf S(y)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
y&0\\
0&\omega\\
0&1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

where the first and second columns correspond to the firm and consumer, respectively.

The steady-state equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model is

$$
\mathbf p^\top\mathbf D(\mathbf p,y,c)
=
\mathbf p^\top\mathbf S(y)
$$

$$
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,y,c)\mathbf 1
=
\mathbf S(y)\mathbf 1
$$

Solving the model gives

$$
l^*=\omega,
\qquad
y^*=c^*=\alpha\omega
$$

and

$$
p_l^*
=
\rho\alpha
$$

$$
p_m^*
=
\frac{1-\rho^2}{\rho}\alpha\omega
$$

The corresponding equilibrium money holdings are

$$
h^{f*}
=
\frac{\rho}{1+\rho},
\qquad
h^{c*}
=
\frac1{1+\rho}
$$

so that

$$
h^{f*}+h^{c*}=1
$$
